chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, all of them, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who was known and virtuous, who died and left a debt upon him which he had been tested by, and he was not a spendthrift, nor a miser, nor well-known for begging. I asked: Is one thousand and two thousand paid off from the khums on his behalf? He said, 'Yes.'

key_terms.الزَّكَاةِ: Khums (one-fifth tax) in this context, referring to the share of khums distributed to the heir.
key_terms.عَارِفٍ فَاضِلٍ: Known and virtuous, describing the character of the deceased.
key_terms.قَدِ اُبْتُلِيَ بِهِ: He was tested by it, indicating the debt was a genuine trial or burden, not due to negligence.
key_terms.مَعْرُوفٌ بِالْمَسْأَلَةِ: Well-known for begging, indicating he did not rely on others for support.
key_terms.مُسْرِفٍ: Miser/stingy, one who hoarded wealth excessively.
key_terms.مُفْسِدٍ: Spendthrift/extravagant, one who wasted wealth unnecessarily.

ai.seo_question: How are the debts of a deceased person paid from their khums share according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies that the deceased's personal debts are prioritized over the distribution of khums to heirs, provided the deceased was not known for extravagance or begging. It highlights the Shia juristic principle that zakat and khums funds can be utilized to settle the financial obligations of the deceased, ensuring their spiritual and material debts are cleared before inheritance distribution.
